title: The price that maximises revenue
objectives: Write revenue as price times quantity and recognise it as a quadratic
Find the best price at the vertex, halfway between the zero-revenue prices

screens.prose: You sell a market-data subscription. At a price of $p$ pounds a month, $500 - 10p$ people subscribe. Each £1.00 rise loses 10 subscribers.
screens.question: Slide the price to bring in as much revenue as you can.

hints.text: Watch the revenue under the chart as you slide.
Revenue rises, peaks, then falls. Find the top.

feedback.correct: £25.00 a month: 250 subscribers and £6,250.00 of revenue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the point is as high as it goes.

byKey.choke: At £50.00 nobody subscribes, so revenue is £0.00.
byKey.free: At £0.00 everyone subscribes but nobody pays anything.

explain.text: Below £25.00 a rise gains more per subscriber than it loses in subscribers. Above it, the lost subscribers cost more. At £25.00 revenue peaks at $25 \times 250 = 6250$ pounds.

screens.prose: Here is the whole revenue curve, $R(p) = p(500 - 10p)$. Drag P along it and compare the heights on either side of the peak.
screens.question: Revenue at £20.00 is £6,000.00. At which other price is it the same?

hints.text: Drag P past the peak until it is back at the same height.
The peak is at £25.00. How far from it is £20.00?
£20.00 is £5.00 below the peak, so try £5.00 above it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the price on the other side of the peak with the same height.

byKey.peak: £25.00 is the peak, with revenue £6,250.00. Go past it to find the same height again.
byKey.double: At £40.00 only 100 subscribe: £4,000.00. The mirror point is as far past the peak as £20.00 is before it.

explain.text: £20.00 and £30.00 are both £5.00 from the peak at £25.00, so they earn the same: $30 \times 200 = 6000$. The revenue curve is a parabola, symmetric about $p = 25$.

screens.prose: Revenue is price times quantity: $R(p) = p(500 - 10p) = 500p - 10p^2$. That is a **quadratic model**, with $a < 0$. A second product has demand $q = 800 - 20p$.
screens.question: Write its revenue $R(p)$ in expanded form.

hints.text: Multiply the price $p$ by the number who subscribe.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $p$ by $800 - 20p$ and expand.

byKey.no-p: That is the demand, the number who subscribe. Multiply by the price $p$.
byKey.form: That is equal, but still in brackets. Multiply it out.

explain.text: Each of the $800 - 20p$ subscribers pays $p$, so $R = p(800 - 20p) = 800p - 20p^2$. The $-20p^2$ makes the curve open downwards. So revenue has a highest point.

screens.prose: $R(p) = p(800 - 20p)$ is already factorised. Revenue is zero when $p = 0$, and again when nobody subscribes.

state.caption: The two zero-revenue prices are marked.

screens.question: Which price maximises revenue?

hints.text: Which two prices give zero revenue?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go halfway between the two prices that give zero revenue.

byKey.choke: At £40.00 nobody subscribes, so revenue is zero there.
byKey.revenue: 8000 is the revenue at the peak. The question asks for the price.
byKey.quarter: You halved twice. The midpoint of 0 and 40 is 20.

explain.text: Revenue is zero at £0.00 and at £40.00, so the peak is halfway, at £20.00. There $R = 20 \times 400 = 8000$ pounds. It is the midpoint rule from the roots lesson.

screens.prose: Completing the square shows the peak directly. Back to the first product: take out $-10$, so $500p - 10p^2 = -10(p^2 - 50p)$.
screens.question: Complete $500p - 10p^2 = -10(p - \square)^2 + \square$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve $-50$ for the bracket, then multiply the leftover by $-10$.

byKey.t50: You put the whole 50 in the bracket. $(p - 50)^2$ gives $-100p$; halve it.
byKey.t625: 625 is the leftover inside the bracket. The $-10$ outside multiplies it: $-10 \times (-625) = 6250$.

explain.text: $-10(p - 25)^2$ is never positive, so revenue is at most 6250 pounds. It reaches 6250 only when $p = 25$. The completed square form shows both facts at once.

screens.prose: A broker sells research notes. At $p$ pounds a note, it sells $1500 - 200p$ notes a week.
screens.question: Which price maximises weekly revenue?

hints.text: Revenue is $p(1500 - 200p)$. Which prices make it zero?
Zero at $p = 0$, and at $1500 - 200p = 0$, which is $p = 7.5$.

feedback.correct: £3.75 a note: 750 notes and £2,812.50 a week.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the two zero-revenue prices and go halfway.

byKey.choke: At £7.50 no notes sell, so revenue is zero.
byKey.revenue: £2,812.50 is the best revenue. The question asks for the price.
byKey.rounded: Prices go to the penny. Halfway between 0 and 7.50 is exactly 3.75.

explain.text: Revenue $p(1500 - 200p)$ is zero at £0.00 and £7.50. Halfway is £3.75, where 750 notes sell. Revenue there is $3.75 \times 750 = 2812.50$ pounds a week.

screens.prose: Back to the subscription: $q = 500 - 10p$, best price £25.00. Now each subscriber costs £4.00 to serve, so profit is $(p - 4)(500 - 10p)$. Sam says: add the cost on and charge £29.00.

state.caption: Revenue is drawn. The profit curve is hidden.

screens.question: Which price maximises profit?

options.why: You passed on the whole £4.00. The zero-profit prices are £4.00 and £50.00, so the peak moves only half as far.

canvas.caption: Profit is lower at £29.00 than at the peak.

options.why: That maximises revenue. The cost moves the left root from 0 to 4.

canvas.caption: The profit peak sits to the right of £25.00.

options.why: You took the cost off the price. A cost pushes the best price up, not down.

canvas.caption: The profit peak sits to the right of £25.00.

hints.text: Which two prices make the profit zero?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the two zero-profit prices and go halfway.

byKey.full-cost: You added the full £4.00. The peak sits halfway between £4.00 and £50.00, so it moves by £2.00.

explain.text: Profit is zero at £4.00 and £50.00, so it peaks halfway, at £27.00. The cost moved one root by £4.00, so the midpoint moved by £2.00. Profit there is $23 \times 230 = 5290$ pounds.

screens.prose: Now take any linear demand, $q = A - Bp$, with $A$ and $B$ positive. Revenue is $R(p) = p(A - Bp)$.
screens.question: Find the price that maximises revenue, in terms of $A$ and $B$.

hints.text: Which two prices give zero revenue?
The peak is halfway between 0 and $\tfrac{A}{B}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the two zero-revenue prices, then go halfway.

byKey.choke: $\tfrac{A}{B}$ is the price where demand reaches zero. The peak is half of it.
byKey.bracket: That reads as $\tfrac{A}{2} \times B$. Type A/(2B), with the brackets, so that $2B$ sits under the line.

explain.text: Revenue is zero at $p = 0$ and at $p = \tfrac{A}{B}$, so the best price is $\tfrac{A}{2B}$. The vertex rule agrees: $R = -Bp^2 + Ap$ gives $-\tfrac{A}{2(-B)}$. Check with $A = 500$ and $B = 10$: £25.00.

screens.prose: With linear demand, revenue is a downward parabola in the price. Its peak is $$p^* = \frac{A}{2B}$$ halfway between £0.00 and the price where demand vanishes. A unit cost $c$ moves the left root to $c$, so the best price becomes $\tfrac{1}{2}\left(c + \tfrac{A}{B}\right)$.
screens.question: Demand is $q = 900 - 30p$. Which price maximises revenue?

options.why: £30.00 is where demand reaches zero, $\tfrac{A}{B}$. Halve it.
You halved 900 and forgot $B$. Divide by $2B = 60$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $p^* = \tfrac{A}{2B}$ with $A = 900$ and $B = 30$.

explain.text: $A = 900$ and $B = 30$, so $p^* = \tfrac{900}{60} = 15$. Demand vanishes at £30.00, and £15.00 is halfway. Revenue there is $15 \times 450 = 6750$ pounds.

screens.prose: Two uncorrelated assets: A with volatility 10%, B with 30%. Putting weight $w$ in A and $1 - w$ in B gives variance $V(w) = 0.1w^2 - 0.18w + 0.09$.
screens.question: Drag P to the weight with the least variance.

hints.text: The least variance is at the vertex.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move P to the bottom of the curve.

byKey.equal: Equal weights give $V = 0.025$. Tilting towards the calmer asset A lowers it further.
byKey.swapped: You put 90% in B, the riskier asset. The vertex is at 0.9 in A.
byKey.P: P is not at the bottom of the curve yet.

explain.text: The vertex is at $w = \tfrac{0.18}{2 \times 0.1} = 0.9$. There $V = 0.009$, a volatility of about 9.5%, below either asset alone. Because the assets are uncorrelated, their moves partly cancel.

ideas: Revenue is price times quantity. With linear demand $q = A - Bp$ it is the quadratic $p(A - Bp)$.
The best price is the vertex, halfway between £0.00 and the price where demand vanishes: $\tfrac{A}{2B}$.
A unit cost moves one root, so the best price rises by half the cost, not all of it.
summary.trap: Adding the full cost to the old best price overshoots. The peak moves by half the cost.

quiz.prose: Demand for a data feed is $q = 600 - 40p$ at a price of $p$ pounds.
quiz.question: Which price maximises revenue?

feedback.correct: £7.50, halfway to the £15.00 where demand vanishes.

byKey.choke: At £15.00 demand is zero. The best price is half of that.
byKey.no-b: You halved 600 and left out $B$. Divide by $2 \times 40$.

explain.text: Revenue $p(600 - 40p)$ is zero at £0.00 and £15.00. Halfway is £7.50. Revenue there is $7.5 \times 300 = 2250$ pounds.
